blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — acarbose alpha-glucosidase inhibitor mechanism
stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed acarbose. Which explanation of its action is most accurate?

options.A: Acarbose reversibly inhibits pancreatic alpha-amylase and intestinal alpha-glucosidases, delaying carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption and lowering postmeal glucose rises.
options.B: Acarbose directly stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin regardless of the current glucose level, producing its main glucose-lowering effect through insulin secretion.
options.C: Acarbose blocks renal SGLT2 transporters, reducing glucose reabsorption and increasing urinary glucose loss as the principal mechanism for lowering plasma glucose.
options.D: Acarbose inhibits DPP-4, prolonging active incretin hormones so glucose-dependent insulin release rises and glucagon secretion falls after meals.

rationale: Current acarbose labeling states that acarbose does not enhance insulin secretion. Its antihyperglycemic action results from competitive, reversible inhibition of pancreatic alpha-amylase and membrane-bound intestinal alpha-glucoside hydrolases, delaying glucose absorption and lowering postprandial hyperglycemia. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly describes direct insulin secretagogue action, C describes an SGLT2 inhibitor, and D describes a DPP-4 inhibitor.
educational_objective: Explain that acarbose lowers postprandial glucose by delaying carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption through pancreatic alpha-amylase and intestinal alpha-glucosidase inhibition rather than by stimulating insulin secretion.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA labeling
source_version_date: DailyMed updated June 18, 2026; current version 24 published June 22, 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Clinical Pharmacology > Mechanism of Action, current DailyMed lines 182-188: acarbose does not enhance insulin secretion; competitive reversible inhibition of pancreatic alpha-amylase and intestinal alpha-glucoside hydrolases delays glucose absorption and lowers postprandial hyperglycemia.
source_claim_supported: Acarbose competitively and reversibly inhibits pancreatic alpha-amylase and intestinal alpha-glucosidases, delaying glucose absorption and lowering postprandial hyperglycemia without enhancing insulin secretion.

candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive antihyperglycemic-mechanism explanations of comparable length.
Preserved the exact local intestinal enzyme-inhibition mechanism and removed the original answer-length cue.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches the current acarbose label. A-C are closely length-matched and D remains a substantive competing mechanism; no second defensible answer remains.
